questions.question: What is parental care?
options: A social behavior that improves offspring survival, growth, and development
A reflex that appears only during pregnancy and disappears after birth
A feeding behavior whose only biological function is providing calories
A fixed instinct that is unaffected by sensory or social experience
questions.feedback: Parental care includes behaviors that increase offspring survival, growth, and acquisition of skills needed for independent life.

questions.question: Which combination best describes major functions of parental care?
options: Nutrition and thermoregulation without any contribution to social development
Protection and sustenance together with opportunities for learning and experience
Predator avoidance and locomotion without effects on physiological regulation
Reproductive competition and mate choice without effects on the offspring
questions.feedback: Parental care can provide food, warmth, protection, physiological regulation, social interaction, and opportunities for learning.

questions.question: Why can parental care increase evolutionary fitness?
options: It guarantees that every offspring survives regardless of environmental conditions
It eliminates the energetic costs associated with producing and raising offspring
It can increase the probability that offspring survive and eventually reproduce
It increases parental fitness only by increasing the number of offspring produced
questions.feedback: Parental investment can increase fitness indirectly by increasing the probability that offspring survive and later reproduce.

questions.question: How should high- and low-investment reproductive strategies be understood?
options: As two fixed biological classes that every species fits into perfectly
As strategies determined only by the number of offspring produced at birth
As patterns that apply only to mammals and not to other vertebrates
As different points along a life-history continuum rather than rigid categories
questions.feedback: High- and low-investment strategies are useful endpoints of a continuum; modern life-history theory is more complex than a strict r/K dichotomy.

questions.question: What is attachment?
options: A stable bond that regulates proximity, safety, stress, and exploration
A temporary feeding preference that disappears once the infant is satiated
A general attraction to any moving object encountered after birth
A purely cognitive judgment about which adult provides the most food
questions.feedback: Attachment is a stable emotional and behavioral bond that helps regulate proximity to the caregiver, safety, stress, and exploration.

questions.question: What does it mean to say that a caregiver acts as a secure base?
options: The caregiver keeps the infant in continuous physical contact and prevents independent exploration
The caregiver provides security that allows the infant to explore the environment
The caregiver becomes the only possible source of physiological regulation throughout early development
The caregiver removes the need to learn about unfamiliar environments and social situations
questions.feedback: A secure base supports exploration: infants are more willing to explore when a familiar attachment figure is available.

questions.question: What was the key result of Harlow's surrogate-mother experiment?
options: Infant monkeys consistently preferred whichever surrogate delivered milk during each feeding period tested
Infant monkeys divided their time approximately equally between the cloth and wire surrogates
Infant monkeys strongly preferred the soft cloth surrogate over the wire surrogate
Infant monkeys avoided both artificial surrogates unless their biological mother was also present
questions.feedback: Infant rhesus monkeys spent far more time with the cloth surrogate, even when the wire surrogate provided food.

questions.question: What did Harlow's findings imply about feeding and attachment?
options: Attachment develops only after infants learn which caregiver reliably provides food during repeated feeding episodes
Feeding is sufficient to explain attachment when the caregiver remains physically close to the infant
Physical contact matters mainly after the infant's nutritional needs have already been fully satisfied
Contact comfort can be a powerful attachment signal independently of feeding
questions.feedback: The results challenged the idea that attachment is simply a secondary consequence of feeding and highlighted contact comfort.

questions.question: What did Harlow's social-isolation studies show?
options: Severe early social deprivation can produce persistent abnormalities in later behavior
Early social deprivation changes behavior only while the period of social isolation is still occurring
Social isolation improves later independence by reducing the young animal's reliance on familiar caregivers
Early deprivation alters feeding behavior but leaves later social and emotional behavior largely unaffected
questions.feedback: Harlow's later work showed that severe early social deprivation can have long-lasting effects on social and emotional behavior.

questions.question: Why is parent-offspring recognition described as multisensory?
options: All species rely on the same sensory cue but weight it differently over time
Different species combine sensory cues such as smell, touch, vision, and vocalizations
Recognition depends on vision in adults and on audition in every newborn animal
Parental recognition occurs without sensory input once maternal hormones are present
questions.feedback: Parent-offspring recognition can depend on different combinations of olfactory, tactile, visual, and vocal cues, with species-specific weighting.

questions.question: What is filial imprinting?
options: A genetically fixed preference that emerges without previous exposure to any particular caregiver-like stimulus
A form of adult social learning that requires repeated reinforcement across many days or weeks
Rapid early learning of a caregiver-like or salient stimulus that guides following behavior
A reflexive response to food that disappears once the young animal begins independent feeding
questions.feedback: Filial imprinting is an early form of learning in which young animals rapidly develop a strong preference for and tendency to follow a salient stimulus.

questions.question: Why is imprinting usually described as having a sensitive period?
options: Learning remains equally effective throughout life but the resulting preference becomes harder to measure later
The preference is completely genetically specified and develops without any relevant early sensory experience
Imprinting begins only after the young animal has reached reproductive maturity and social independence
Learning is especially effective during an early window but is not absolutely irreversible
questions.feedback: Imprinting is strongest during an early developmental window, but later work showed more flexibility than a strictly irreversible critical period would imply.

questions.question: Which brain region is strongly implicated in visual imprinting in domestic chicks?
options: The intermediate medial mesopallium (IMM)
The medial preoptic area of the hypothalamus
The ventral pallidum of the basal forebrain
The accessory olfactory bulb of the forebrain
questions.feedback: The intermediate medial mesopallium (IMM) is strongly involved in visual imprinting in domestic chicks.

questions.question: What happens to neuronal responses in the IMM after imprinting?
options: Responses become equally strong for every familiar and unfamiliar object
Responses become selectively enhanced for the object used during imprinting
Neurons stop responding to visual stimuli once the preference is learned
Responses shift entirely from visual stimuli to maternal olfactory cues
questions.feedback: Imprinting produces stimulus-specific changes in IMM activity, with stronger responses to the learned imprinting object.

questions.question: Why is attachment in newborn rats strongly dependent on odor learning?
options: Olfaction is the only sensory system that remains functional from birth throughout the entire lifespan
Rat pups cannot acquire tactile information until after vision and hearing have reached mature function
Pups must orient to the mother before vision and hearing are fully functional
Maternal odors directly activate motor responses without requiring experience-dependent plasticity in developing sensory circuits
questions.feedback: In newborn rats, olfactory cues are especially important because pups need to orient to the mother before vision and hearing are fully mature.

questions.question: Which neuromodulator strongly supports early odor learning in neonatal rats?
options: Dopamine released from the ventral pallidum
Oxytocin released from the olfactory bulb
Corticosterone released from the hippocampus
Norepinephrine released from the locus coeruleus
questions.feedback: Norepinephrine from the locus coeruleus strongly modulates plasticity in the neonatal olfactory bulb.

questions.question: What can produce a learned odor preference in neonatal rats?
options: Pairing an odor with maternal-like tactile stimulation during the early sensitive window
Presenting an odor repeatedly without accompanying tactile stimulation during later adult life
Pairing a visual pattern with food after the visual system has reached mature function
Blocking plasticity in the olfactory bulb while repeatedly presenting a familiar maternal odor
questions.feedback: Pairing an odor with maternal-like tactile stimulation can produce a learned odor preference, particularly during an early sensitive period.

questions.question: What is important for selective lamb recognition by a mother sheep?
options: Visual imprinting in the intermediate medial mesopallium of the forebrain
Olfactory information and noradrenergic signaling in the maternal olfactory bulb
Suppression of all olfactory input immediately after the lamb is born
Learning the lamb's identity only after several weeks of nursing
questions.feedback: Mother sheep rapidly learn the identity of their lamb, and this recognition depends strongly on olfactory information and noradrenergic signaling in the maternal olfactory bulb.

questions.question: Which set contains characteristic components of rodent maternal behavior?
options: Courtship display, territorial marking, predatory behavior, and long-distance migratory navigation in adulthood
Visual imprinting, song learning, flocking behavior, and long-distance spatial homing
Pup retrieval, licking and grooming, arched-back nursing, and nest building
Object recognition, food hoarding, burrowing behavior, and dominance-related aggressive interactions
questions.feedback: Rodent maternal behavior includes pup retrieval, licking and grooming, arched-back nursing, and nest building.

questions.question: Why are rats and mice useful models for studying parental care?
options: Their maternal behavior is completely independent of hormones and sensory input
Their offspring develop without requiring any direct contact with the mother
Their parental behavior is identical across all individuals and environmental conditions
Their maternal behaviors are stereotyped, quantifiable, and experimentally accessible
questions.feedback: Rodent maternal behaviors can be reliably observed and quantified, making them useful for studying neural and developmental mechanisms.

questions.question: Which hormones are highlighted as helping prepare the maternal brain around parturition?
options: Estradiol, progesterone, prolactin, and oxytocin
Cortisol, insulin, melatonin, and growth hormone
Dopamine, serotonin, glutamate, and acetylcholine
Testosterone, thyroxine, adrenaline, and vasopressin
questions.feedback: Estradiol, progesterone, prolactin, and oxytocin are important endocrine signals around the onset of maternal behavior.

questions.question: How do pregnancy-related hormones influence maternal behavior?
options: They act as a single irreversible switch that automatically produces maternal care
They alter the responsiveness of neural circuits processing pups and maternal motivation
They eliminate the need for sensory cues from offspring after parturition
They control maternal behavior only by changing milk production in the mammary gland
questions.feedback: Pregnancy-related hormones prepare the maternal brain by changing the responsiveness of circuits that process pup-related sensory signals and motivation.

questions.question: Which endocrine pattern occurs near parturition in the rat?
options: Progesterone rises sharply while estradiol and prolactin both disappear
All three hormones remain constant from early pregnancy through parturition
Progesterone falls while estradiol and prolactin rise around delivery
Estradiol falls to zero while progesterone remains maximal after delivery
questions.feedback: Near parturition, progesterone falls while estradiol rises and prolactin shows a marked increase, accompanying the onset of maternal behavior.

questions.question: What is the role of the medial preoptic area (MPOA) in maternal behavior?
options: It processes retinal orientation selectivity used for visually recognizing the pups
It generates corticosterone in response to pup-related stress during nursing
It stores the olfactory memory of an imprinted object in young chicks
It integrates hormonal, sensory, motivational, and reward-related information relevant to caregiving
questions.feedback: The MPOA is a major node in the maternal neural network and integrates hormonal state, pup-related sensory signals, and motivational information.

questions.question: What effect does disrupting MPOA function have in rodents?
options: It strongly impairs the expression of maternal behavior
It selectively improves pup retrieval while reducing other components of maternal behavior
It increases care by removing olfactory avoidance
It changes filial imprinting without altering maternal caregiving
questions.feedback: Disrupting MPOA function strongly impairs maternal behavior, supporting its central role in the caregiving network.

questions.question: Which pathway is associated with maternal motivation in the maternal neural network?
options: The intermediate medial mesopallium activates the hippocampus, pituitary, adrenal cortex, and hypothalamus
MPOA activity engages the VTA, nucleus accumbens, and ventral pallidum
The olfactory bulb directly activates corticospinal motor pathways
The visual cortex activates the amygdala, retina, and superior colliculus
questions.feedback: An MPOA-to-VTA-to-nucleus-accumbens pathway engages ventral pallidum circuitry involved in maternal motivation.

questions.question: How can the MPOA/BNST promote maternal behavior besides activating reward-related pathways?
options: It can suppress all sensory processing of pup-related cues
It can eliminate the hormonal changes associated with parturition
It can suppress neural pathways that promote pup avoidance
It can prevent learning of the pups' olfactory characteristics
questions.feedback: The maternal network includes suppression of avoidance-related pathways involving hypothalamic regions and the PAG.

questions.question: What is maternal sensitization?
options: The rapid loss of maternal behavior after pups are briefly removed from the nest
The hormonal induction of maternal behavior that occurs only during pregnancy
The formation of a selective visual imprint on pups immediately after birth
The gradual emergence of maternal behavior in virgin females after repeated pup exposure
questions.feedback: Repeated exposure to pups can gradually induce maternal behavior in virgin female rats even without pregnancy; this is termed maternal sensitization.

questions.question: What happens when olfactory input is reduced in virgin rats exposed to pups?
options: Maternal behavior can emerge more rapidly because an avoidance-related influence is reduced
Maternal behavior disappears because pup odors are the only signals that can trigger care
Maternal behavior becomes impossible unless visual input is simultaneously removed
Pup retrieval increases only after olfactory function has fully recovered
questions.feedback: Reducing olfactory input can accelerate maternal behavior in virgin rats, consistent with pup odors initially engaging avoidance or inhibitory pathways.

questions.question: Which maternal behaviors are used to describe naturally occurring differences in rodent caregiving style?
options: Pup retrieval and visual imprinting responses
Licking/grooming and arched-back nursing
Nest building and predator-avoidance behavior
Courtship displays and territorial aggressive behavior
questions.feedback: Natural variation in licking/grooming and arched-back nursing is used to characterize different levels of maternal care in rats.

questions.question: What is associated with relatively high maternal licking/grooming and arched-back nursing?
options: Lower hippocampal GR expression and weaker glucocorticoid negative feedback
Higher ACTH and corticosterone responses that remain elevated for longer
Higher hippocampal GR expression and stronger glucocorticoid negative feedback
Complete elimination of the offspring HPA response to acute stress
questions.feedback: High LG/ABN offspring show higher hippocampal glucocorticoid receptor expression and stronger negative feedback regulation of the HPA axis.

questions.question: How do adult stress responses differ after high versus low maternal care?
options: High-care offspring show larger and more prolonged ACTH and corticosterone responses
Low-care offspring show no hormonal response to an acute stressor in adulthood
Maternal care alters behavior but has no measurable effect on stress hormones
High-care offspring show smaller and more rapidly declining ACTH and corticosterone responses
questions.feedback: Offspring receiving high LG/ABN show smaller and more rapidly terminated ACTH and corticosterone responses to acute stress.

questions.question: What does the HPA-axis result show about early maternal care?
options: Early caregiving can produce long-lasting changes in physiological stress regulation
Maternal care affects only immediate behavior while pups remain in the nest
Stress physiology is fixed genetically and is unaffected by early social experience
Only adult social experience can alter the endocrine response to acute stress
questions.feedback: Variation in early maternal care is associated with persistent differences in regulation of the HPA stress axis.

questions.question: What is the purpose of cross-fostering between high- and low-care mothers?
options: To increase genetic differences between litters before measuring maternal behavior
To separate effects of the rearing environment from biological parentage
To prevent mothers from expressing their characteristic caregiving styles
To eliminate all postnatal social experience while preserving prenatal influences
questions.feedback: Cross-fostering allows researchers to distinguish effects associated with the rearing mother from those associated with biological origin.

questions.question: What does cross-fostering show about offspring stress physiology and behavior?
options: They always resemble the biological mother regardless of the foster environment
They become intermediate between the two mothers regardless of caregiving level
They tend to resemble patterns associated with the rearing mother's caregiving style
They are unaffected by either maternal style once genetic background is controlled
questions.feedback: Cross-fostering shifts offspring outcomes toward those associated with the foster mother's caregiving style.

questions.question: What is meant by nongenomic transmission of maternal style?
options: A new mutation is produced in offspring whenever maternal care is unusually high
The maternal genome is physically transferred to the offspring during licking and grooming
Maternal behavior is inherited only through mitochondrial DNA from the biological mother
A caregiving pattern can pass across generations through developmental experience rather than DNA sequence change
questions.feedback: Female offspring can later reproduce the caregiving style they experienced, and cross-fostering can shift this pattern without changing DNA sequence.

questions.question: What is epigenetics in the context of the maternal-care experiments?
options: Regulation of gene activity without changing the underlying DNA sequence
Permanent alteration of DNA sequence caused by tactile stimulation from the mother
Replacement of inherited genes by newly synthesized genes during early development
A change in chromosome number produced by prolonged activation of the stress system
questions.feedback: Epigenetic mechanisms regulate how accessible or active genes are without altering the underlying DNA sequence.

questions.question: What is the usual relationship between promoter DNA methylation and gene expression?
options: Higher promoter methylation always increases transcription of the nearby gene
Higher promoter methylation is commonly associated with lower gene expression
Promoter methylation changes the DNA sequence so the gene encodes a new protein
Promoter methylation affects only histone synthesis and not transcriptional accessibility
questions.feedback: In the simplified framework used here, higher methylation near a promoter is usually associated with reduced accessibility and reduced gene expression.

questions.question: How can histone modifications regulate gene expression?
options: They replace DNA bases and permanently rewrite the nucleotide sequence
They determine which sensory receptor proteins are transported into the retina
They can alter chromatin accessibility and thereby influence transcription
They remove chromosomes from cells that receive little maternal stimulation
questions.feedback: Chemical modifications to histone tails can make chromatin more open or compact, changing how accessible genes are to transcriptional machinery.

questions.question: What effect is associated with high maternal care at the hippocampal glucocorticoid receptor gene?
options: Increased promoter methylation and reduced glucocorticoid receptor expression
Deletion of the receptor gene followed by compensatory receptor synthesis
Permanent silencing of all genes involved in the HPA stress response
Reduced promoter methylation and increased glucocorticoid receptor expression
questions.feedback: High maternal care is associated with reduced methylation at a glucocorticoid receptor promoter and increased GR expression.

questions.question: What role does NGFI-A/EGR1 play in the maternal-care pathway?
options: It acts as a transcription factor whose access to the GR promoter is facilitated by high care
It acts as a stress hormone released by the adrenal gland after acute restraint
It acts as a neurotransmitter released from the locus coeruleus during odor learning
It acts as a DNA methyltransferase that silences the glucocorticoid receptor gene
questions.feedback: High maternal care is associated with greater access of NGFI-A/EGR1 to regulatory regions of the glucocorticoid receptor gene.

questions.question: What does the gene Nr3c1 encode in the maternal-care example?
options: The serotonin 5-HT7 receptor
The glucocorticoid receptor
The prolactin receptor
The oxytocin receptor
questions.feedback: Nr3c1 is the gene encoding the glucocorticoid receptor (GR).

questions.question: How does increased hippocampal glucocorticoid receptor expression affect the HPA axis?
options: It blocks all hypothalamic activity and prevents any stress response from beginning
It increases ACTH secretion so corticosterone remains elevated for a longer period
It strengthens glucocorticoid negative feedback and helps terminate the stress response
It weakens feedback from circulating glucocorticoids to the brain and pituitary
questions.feedback: Higher hippocampal GR expression strengthens negative feedback, contributing to a smaller and more rapidly terminated hormonal stress response.

questions.question: What pattern is associated with relatively low maternal care?
options: Lower GR-promoter methylation, higher GR expression, and faster stress recovery
Higher GR expression with complete suppression of ACTH and corticosterone release
No epigenetic differences and no change in adult stress-related physiology
Greater GR-promoter methylation, lower GR expression, and a more prolonged stress response
questions.feedback: Low maternal care is associated with greater methylation at the GR promoter, lower GR expression, and more prolonged HPA-axis responses.

questions.question: Which statement best describes epigenetic programming?
options: It can be persistent while remaining potentially modifiable by later biological influences
It is always permanent once established during the first days of life
It changes DNA sequence and therefore cannot be modified in adult animals
It disappears completely when the offspring leaves the maternal nest
questions.feedback: Epigenetic regulation can persist into adulthood while still remaining potentially modifiable by later biological influences.

questions.question: What can brief handling of rodent pups produce in some paradigms?
options: Permanent loss of maternal behavior and increased stress responses in every strain
More maternal interaction after reunion and reduced later stress reactivity
Complete independence from maternal care immediately after the handling period
Irreversible suppression of the HPA axis throughout the rest of development
questions.feedback: Brief separations can increase maternal interaction after reunion and, in some rodent paradigms, are associated with reduced later stress reactivity.

questions.question: How can prolonged repeated maternal separation differ from brief handling?
options: It reliably increases maternal interaction without producing any later stress-related effects
It has the same developmental consequences as brief handling regardless of duration
It can act as an early-life stressor with persistent physiological and behavioral effects
It affects only body growth while leaving stress-related physiology unchanged
questions.feedback: Longer repeated separations can function as early-life stressors and can produce persistent changes in stress-related physiology and behavior.

questions.question: Why can the effects of maternal separation vary across experiments?
options: They depend only on whether the offspring are male or female at birth
They are determined entirely by the mother's genotype and not by the procedure
They vary only because stress hormones cannot be measured reliably in rodents
They depend on duration, age, strain, housing, and what happens after reunion
questions.feedback: The effects of separation depend on duration, developmental age, strain, housing, and maternal behavior after reunion.

questions.question: What is the most appropriate interpretation of long-lasting effects of early maternal care?
options: Early care can bias developmental trajectories without rigidly determining a single adult outcome
Early care permanently fixes adult behavior so later experience has no meaningful influence
Early care has no lasting influence because all developmental effects disappear by adulthood
Only genetic inheritance determines adult outcomes once the offspring has been born
questions.feedback: Early maternal care can shape neural, endocrine, and epigenetic development, but later experience can continue to modify outcomes.

questions.question: Which statement best summarizes the relation between early and later experience?
options: Later environments completely erase all consequences of early caregiving without exception
Early experience creates developmental biases that can still interact with later environments
Early caregiving determines adult outcomes independently of all later social experience
Early and later experiences affect separate systems and therefore cannot interact
questions.feedback: Early experience can bias development, while later social environment, enrichment, stress, and relationships can still interact with that developmental state.
